mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Thursday, November 19, 2026. The most urgent story today concerns a series of unexplained technical outages hitting major U.S. infrastructure, including the FAA, NASA, and financial platforms. While there is public speculation regarding potential AI-driven cyberattacks, officials from the Director of National Intelligence and the White House have characterized these as individual, non-coordinated events. Industry experts offer a different perspective: these disruptions may be the growing pains of legacy systems struggling to integrate with modern, AI-augmented infrastructure. Software engineer Anusha Iyer and cybersecurity veteran Dave DeWalt both suggest that the current wave of outages is largely due to hurried attempts to modernize outdated systems. As organizations rush to patch vulnerabilities surfaced by rapidly deployed AI tools, the friction between legacy hardware and modern software is creating widespread instability. Iyer, for instance, noted that the recent FAA outage likely stemmed from a failure to properly support legacy hardware while transitioning to advanced telecommunications infrastructure. DeWalt added that while these vulnerabilities have long existed, the rapid speed at which AI identifies them is forcing enterprises to engage in a surge of patching that triggers short-term operational disruptions. In infrastructure developments, Amazon has introduced a new monitoring feature for SageMaker AI, designed to address the common problem of endpoint drift. As generative AI models remain in production, they often become less efficient due to shifting traffic patterns or new software releases. SageMaker AI will now automatically observe operational signals—such as latency and GPU utilization—to detect when a configuration could be improved. The system provides plain-language notifications through AWS Health, allowing users to benchmark their current setup against optimized alternatives without altering the production environment until they choose to do so. This feature is enabled by default for specific container types to help developers lower costs and maintain performance. By monitoring latency drift and unused capacity, this tool helps prevent silent performance degradation, ensuring that compute resources are managed efficiently rather than sitting idle. Separately, NVIDIA and Microsoft have expanded their collaborative efforts in accelerated computing. At the Microsoft Ignite conference, the companies announced that NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are now available in Azure data centers to support large-scale model training and agentic applications. This partnership also extends to Windows PCs and aims to improve power efficiency in data centers through new software technologies. Additionally, Microsoft is utilizing NVIDIA’s inference software and Blackwell GPUs to enhance its own internal models, including those powering Bing search, as both firms look to strengthen the underlying infrastructure for enterprise AI deployment. These advancements in confidential computing and power management are intended to provide a more secure and efficient foundation for businesses deploying proprietary AI models. In other news, Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Neon, a new model focused on complex reasoning and software engineering. It is currently available through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, with Google reporting high rankings on benchmarks for scientific and mathematical tasks. This model is designed to handle multi-step instruction following and long-horizon tasks, such as those found in software refactoring and corporate data analysis. Hugging Face researchers have released findings from an analysis of 272 production fine-tuning jobs. Their work suggests that traditional, FLOP-based calculations are poor predictors of how long fine-tuning will take, with a machine learning regressor proving significantly more accurate by accounting for variables like checkpoint policies and memory overheads. By moving away from inaccurate estimates, developers can better schedule jobs on shared clusters, reducing the amount of time that expensive GPU resources sit idle. The startup Osmo is claiming human-level olfactory intelligence for its AI model, which aims to digitize the sense of smell. Using a dataset derived from human labelers and chemical sensors, the company is already working with the fragrance industry to design new scents.
